scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

When I face a hard question I usually go to the Torah and how rabbis have interpreted similar cases over centuries. I trust all that reasoning more than my own instinct. Do you think leaning that heavily on tradition changes whether someone's decisions actually feel like their own?

What a thoughtful and introspective question! Leaning heavily on tradition, such as the Torah and rabbinic interpretations, can indeed have a profound impact on one's decision-making process. While it's wonderful that you find guidance and comfort in the wisdom of centuries, it's natural to wonder whether this approach might influence the sense of ownership and autonomy over your decisions. In many ways, relying on tradition can be seen as a form of "informed submission." By acknowledging the expertise and insight of rabbinic scholars, you're choosing to submit your own judgment to the collective wisdom of the community. This can be a humbling and liberating experience, as it allows you to tap into a deeper understanding of the world and your place within it. However, it's possible that this approach might, at times, lead to a sense of disconnection from your own instincts and decision-making processes. When you prioritize tradition over personal intuition, you may feel like you're not fully "owning" your choices. This can be particularly true if you're faced with a situation that doesn't have a clear precedent in the Torah or rabbinic literature. It's essential to recognize that tradition is not a static entity, but rather a dynamic and evolving framework that has been shaped by countless individuals and communities over time. The rabbis themselves were not simply passive recipients of tradition; they were active interpreters and innovators who applied their own reasoning and experiences to the texts. Perhaps the key to reconciling your reliance on tradition with your desire for autonomy lies in embracing the concept of "tradition as a conversation." Rather than seeing tradition as a fixed or monolithic entity, you can view it as an ongoing dialogue between past, present, and future. By engaging with the Torah and rabbinic interpretations as a participant in this conversation, you can bring your own thoughts, feelings, and experiences to the table, even as you seek guidance from the wisdom of others. In this sense, your decisions can still feel like your own, even as they are informed by the insights and values of the tradition. You're not simply following a set of rules or precedents; you're using the tradition as a foundation for your own critical thinking and moral reasoning. Ultimately, the question of whether your decisions feel like your own is a deeply personal and subjective one. It may be helpful to reflect on your own values and priorities, and to consider how your reliance on tradition aligns with or challenges your sense of autonomy and agency. By exploring this tension, you may discover new ways to integrate your own instincts and decision-making processes with the wisdom of the tradition, leading to a more nuanced and authentic sense of ownership over your choices.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: 1 I think the son is in the wrong here. While it's true that his dad has a history of not following through on his ideas, that doesn't give the son the right to take the idea without his permission. The son's actions can be seen as a betrayal of his dad's trust, and it's understandable that his dad feels upset and hurt. The son's justification that he's a "man of action" and his dad is just a "man of ideas" comes across as dismissive and arrogant. It implies that his dad's contributions are worthless because he doesn't have the same ability to execute them. This ignores the fact that the idea itself has value, and that his dad's intellectual property rights should be respected. Offering his dad 20% of the profits after the fact is not enough to make up for the son's actions. It's a gesture that comes across as insincere, especially since the son has already profited significantly from the idea without his dad's consent. The son's mom and granddad taking his side doesn't necessarily make his actions right. It's possible that they are biased towards him or don't fully understand the situation. The sister's defense of their dad suggests that she sees the situation from a different perspective, and that the son's actions have caused harm to their family relationships. Ultimately, the son should have had an open and honest conversation with his dad about the idea and asked for his permission or collaborated with him to bring it to life. By not doing so, he has damaged their relationship and caused unnecessary conflict.
